title: Energy Sector Deep Dive Analysis

evidence.title: Post-COVID inflation policy response
evidence.finding: Fed began tapering purchases in November 2021, ended purchases in March 2022 and then raised policy rates; subsequent balance-sheet runoff replaced expansion. This differs from formal yield caps.

claims.reason: Later research found some employment effect from ending benefits, supporting a contribution. The effect was modest relative to lost income and chiefly related to eligibility expiration, not a simple dollar-for-dollar wage substitution.

evidence.title: Early withdrawal of pandemic unemployment insurance
evidence.publisher: Coombs et al., AEA Papers and Proceedings
evidence.finding: Study of 16,253 benefit recipients found early-ending states had UI receipt fall 36.3 percentage points and employment rise 6.8 points by early September. Average cumulative earnings rose $292 versus $2,529 in lost UI. Effects mainly reflected eligibility expiration rather than benefit-level reductions.

claims.reason: Receiving checks while employed avoids the direct benefit-loss mechanism, but income effects can still influence work choices. Saying there is no relevant incentive at all is stronger than the eligibility arithmetic.
claims.mechanism_assessment: Outcome evidence does not independently identify causation.

evidence.title: Global Energy Review 2025
evidence.finding: Global demand rose for oil, gas, coal, renewables and nuclear in 2024. Renewables supplied the largest share of energy-supply growth, while fossil-fuel consumption also increased. This supports additive near-term demand, not an impossibility of future displacement.

claims.reason: Territorial energy use omits energy embodied in imports, but attributing all export production to destination consumers requires input-output accounting. It does not imply efficiency and electrification cannot lower consumption.
claims.mechanism_assessment: Outcome evidence does not independently identify causation.

claims.reason: Recent global demand grew across old and new sources, supporting the observation. Historical addition does not establish that displacement is physically impossible; EVs already displaced some oil demand relative to a counterfactual.
claims.mechanism_assessment: Outcome evidence does not independently identify causation.

framework_lessons: Security access matters alongside business value.
assessment: Energy-sector direction and the lumber reversal warning were supported. The analysis was weaker when translating historical energy addition into a constraint on displacement, and Russian security access was a major risk outside operating fundamentals. The inflation call succeeded while the quoted Bitcoin timing call did not.
